summary:
The page first closes the chapter introduction: after this chapter you will have an intuitive understanding of the mathematical theory behind deep learning and be ready for the modern frameworks introduced in chapter 3 (p.84).

The sidebar **Running the code in this book** explains the book's practical setup. Every chapter is paired with a **Jupyter notebook** containing all of its code — a 'live Python scratch pad' where you can run code interactively, graph data and view images. The authors urge you to run and experiment with the code as you read. The easiest environment is **Google Colaboratory (Colab)**, a hosted notebook service that has become the industry standard for ML practitioners; it runs in the browser on cloud runtimes with configurable hardware, and by default the book's notebooks use **Colab's free GPU runtime**. You can also run locally; a **GPU is recommended**, especially for the larger, more compute-intensive models later in the book. Code and instructions are at `https://github.com/fchollet/deep-learning-with-python-notebooks`.

**Section 2.1, A first look at a neural network**, begins the concrete example: a network built with **Keras** — a simple, high-level library used throughout the book — that learns to classify handwritten digits. The authors warn that unless you already know Keras you won't understand everything immediately; that's fine, since the next sections review each element in detail, so some steps may look like magic for now.

The problem: classify **grayscale images of handwritten digits, 28 × 28 pixels, into 10 categories (0–9)**. The dataset is **MNIST**, a classic almost as old as the field itself: **60,000 training images plus 10,000 test images**, assembled by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (the NIST in MNIST) in the 1980s. 'Solving' MNIST is the **'Hello World' of deep learning** — what you do to verify that your algorithms work — and you will see it over and over in papers and blog posts. Sample digits are shown in figure 2.1 on the next page.

paragraphs.excerpt: The problem we’re trying to solve here is to classify grayscale images
paragraphs.what_it_says: The task: classify grayscale images of handwritten digits (28 × 28 pixels) into 10 categories (0–9) using MNIST, a classic dataset almost as old as the field and intensively studied: 60,000 training images plus 10,000 test images, assembled by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (the NIST in MNIST) in the 1980s. paragraphs.what_it_means: This paragraph fixes the numbers that become tensor shapes on the following pages: 60,000 images × 28 × 28 pixels for training (`(60000, 28, 28)`), 10,000 × 28 × 28 for test, and 10 output classes. paragraphs.why_it_matters: MNIST is small enough to train in seconds yet real enough to exhibit every concept of the chapter (tensors, batches, loss, gradient descent, overfitting). concepts.name: MNIST dataset
concepts.definition: A classic dataset of grayscale handwritten-digit images, 28 × 28 pixels, labeled 0–9: 60,000 training images and 10,000 test images, assembled by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in the 1980s.
concepts.intuition: The 'Hello World' of deep learning — the first program you run to check that everything works.
concepts.technical: Inputs are 28 × 28 = 784 intensity values per image; outputs are one of 10 classes. In Keras it is preloaded as four NumPy arrays (p.42): training images and labels, test images and labels.
concepts.significance: It is the running example of chapter 2 and recurs throughout the machine-learning literature, so its shapes and sizes are worth memorizing.
concepts.example: A training-image tensor of shape (60000, 28, 28) and a label array of 60,000 digits.
concepts.misconception: That doing well on MNIST demonstrates a strong model. The page frames it as a sanity check, not a benchmark of modern capability.

concepts.name: Keras
concepts.definition: A simple, high-level machine learning library used extensively throughout the book to build and train neural networks.
concepts.intuition: A library whose lines map onto concepts (layers, loss, optimizer) rather than onto low-level plumbing.
concepts.technical: Keras runs on top of TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX (p.22); chapter 3 (p.84) describes these frameworks and how core concepts translate to Keras APIs.
concepts.significance: Choosing a high-level library lets chapter 2 present a complete working model in a few lines before explaining it piece by piece.
concepts.misconception: That Keras hides so much that one cannot learn the mathematics from it. Section 2.5 (p.77) reimplements the same example from low-level operations to show exactly what Keras does.

concepts.name: Notebook-based workflow (Jupyter, Colab)
concepts.definition: Running the book's code as Jupyter notebooks — interactive documents of runnable cells — most easily on Google Colab's hosted runtimes with a free GPU, or locally with a GPU recommended.
concepts.intuition: A live scratch pad: run a cell, see the tensor shape or plot, change something, run again.
concepts.technical: Each chapter has one notebook with all its code at https://github.com/fchollet/deep-learning-with-python-notebooks. Colab provides cloud runtimes with configurable hardware; the notebooks default to the free GPU runtime.
concepts.significance: The authors say you gain far more practical knowledge by running and experimenting with the code as you read; the book is literate programming (p.22).
concepts.example: Opening the chapter 2 notebook in Colab and executing `train_images.shape` (p.42).
concepts.misconception: That a GPU is required to follow chapter 2. It is recommended mainly for the larger models later in the book.

concepts.name: Training set vs. test set
concepts.definition: The division of a dataset into data the model learns from (training set) and separate data used to measure how well it performs (test set).
concepts.intuition: Study with one set of exercises, sit the exam with another — otherwise you only measure memorization.
concepts.technical: For MNIST: 60,000 training images, 10,000 test images. The page introduces the split as a property of the dataset; p.42 explains the workflow (train on `train_images`/`train_labels`, test on `test_images`/`test_labels`).
concepts.significance: Evaluating on held-out data is the basis of every generalization measurement in the book.
concepts.example: A model that reaches high accuracy on the 60,000 training digits is only trusted once it performs well on the 10,000 unseen test digits.
concepts.misconception: That the test set may be used for tuning; later chapters introduce a separate validation set for that purpose.

deeper.title: The MNIST numbers as tensor shapes
deeper.body:
The page gives every number needed to predict the shapes you will see on p.42 and later (the shapes themselves appear on p.42; the arithmetic here is mine):

- Training images: 60,000 images, each 28 × 28 → a rank-3 tensor of shape `(60000, 28, 28)` holding 60,000 × 784 = **47,040,000** pixel values.
- Test images: `(10000, 28, 28)` → 7,840,000 values.
- Training labels: 60,000 integers in 0–9 → shape `(60000,)`.
- Classes: 10, so the network's final layer will output 10 scores per image.

Because the images are grayscale there is no color axis; a color image would add a channel dimension (see section 2.2.8, p.50).

deeper.title: Why 'Hello World'?
deeper.body: A 'Hello World' program does nothing interesting; its purpose is to confirm that the compiler, the editor and the run command all work. MNIST plays the same role for a deep-learning setup: the data loads in one line, a small network trains in seconds, and an accuracy near 98% confirms that the framework, the data pipeline and the training loop are wired correctly. If something is wrong with your environment or your understanding, MNIST will reveal it cheaply — which is why the authors say it is what you do 'to verify that your algorithms are working as expected', and why it keeps appearing in papers and blog posts as a quick check rather than as a claim of achievement.
